messages.subject: error trapping when using jagsUI
messages.body_plain:
Hello all

I have a general question relating error trapping when one uses jagsUI (especially when the model is fairly complicated with lots of random effects).  I am running a model using R and using the jagsUI package. I am actually running the following code (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12399/abstract) on someones data set.

I eventually got the following error:

Error in jags.model(file = model.file, data = data, inits = inits, n.chains = n.chains,  :
  Error in node y[124,2]
Node inconsistent with parents

>From experience I know that this has got to do with the fact that the observed y value does not match with the MCMC simulated parameters (i.e. say y~bern(p), y value could be 0 but p is sampled as being 1) .

In this case does anyone know if one is able to obtain the actual samples from a jags call? i.e. if you run something and you receive an error message you will not get any samples stored. Is there a way of actually storing the samples while the MCMC is running so that afterwards one is able to analyse where exactly one is having problems?

Regards

messages.subject: RE: error trapping when using jagsUI
messages.body_plain:
Dear Allan,

this is the worst error message in JAGS possible. As far as I know, the "inconsistent node" error ONLY happens with the initial values, so usually you get rid of it when you choose your inits smartly. However, I have had cases where I could never get to run a model, because I could never find inits that satisfied JAGS. Typically in some sort of population dynamics, where, say, the number of recruits and survivors put strong constraints on the range of possible values of observed data.

Perhaps you can run the model with Win- and OpenBUGS first, for a couple of iterations, then take the last values of each chain as inits for a run in JAGS ?

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Re: error trapping when using jagsUI
messages.body_plain:
Hi Allan,

I agree with Marc, this is always a frustrating error.

I think this question is probably less related to jagsUI specifically, and more related to the rjags package and JAGS (around which jagsUI is just a set of simple wrapper functions).

Based on the error you have given, it appears that the problem is occurring during model compilation and initialization (which is the function of jags.model). If that's the case, it is my understanding that no MCMC samples have yet been generated by JAGS to dump, it's simply comparing the specified parameter initial values with the data and finding an inconsistency (see discussion here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27167416/is-there-a-way-to-dump-jags-node-values-for-debug-purposes).

JAGS apparently immediately deletes models when they fail to compile. It would be helpful to know the exact set of initial values for all parents JAGS was using when compilation errors occur, but that functionality apparently does not exist. There's currently an open ticket requesting this in JAGS, but it's fairly old: https://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/bugs/36/.

One possible solution in addition to those Marc described, would be to manually calculate all the initial 'parents'  in R based on your set of specified input initial values to see if any unrealistic values appear (see example in the JAGS ticket I linked above). Alternatively, you could remove y[] from the model and run the model for a few iterations to see how the 'parent' values are initially behaving.

On the other hand, if your model successfully compiled and was updating and the error occurred while updating, that's a slightly different problem. Supposedly if an error occurs while updating JAGS will dump the current model state into a 'jags.dumpN.R' file, but I have never actually had this happen.

Ken

messages.subject: A cautionary note on Rhat in convergence assessment
messages.subject_clean: A cautionary note on Rhat in convergence assessment
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

here's a cautionary thought for Pentecost: in MCMC-based analyses it's ALWAYS necessary to gauge convergence not only by numerical means with Rhat, but also visually, by looking at the traceplots of the chains or some of the chains. Attached is a Cautionary Plot (obtained via JAGS per jagsUI), where Rhat indicates convergence, but the plot shows a very conspicuous trend and thus that we're still far from convergence.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marc,

you are right, I've seen (I think on stats.stackexchange.com <http://stats.stackexchange.com>) even more
worrying examples of how Rhat would be low on non-converged chains. Cannot
find it, but it was actually an example where the chains did not converge
(in your example, they still converge together, just not to the posterior).

BUT, looking at the chains is not a solution for me. Sometimes I had to
produce HUNDREDS of models and checking each one visually is not the way to
go.

What about PSRF (potential scale reduction factor), generated by
gelman.diag() in package CODA (and reported in package runjags for example)?
Is it the same as Rhat? Does it have the same problem?

Thanks and best wishes!

	Tomas

I will really appreciate your comments.

Best regards

Pablo

Dear Tomas,

I don't know how the multivariate PSRF ("one number for one model") works, but I think it is presumably a multivariate version of the single-parameter Rhat.

I do think that even when you have hundreds of models, one should at least skim over the traceplots of some of the key params or even all.

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Pablo,

I think it’s the same. They define the likelihood of the model using the ones trick or the zeroes trick, which is fine, while we define it hierarchically, which I think is easier to read and to understand for non-statisticians.

But: it would be easy enough to try both out and see whether you get the same answers.

Best regards  --- Marc

Hi everybody,

I have recently started using time-to-detection models, but I am struggling a little bit with the different model specifications that I have found published. My question is, is the model in page 615 of the Applied Hierarchical Modeling book the same described by Georgia Garrard? From my interpretation of the text in the book, it seems to me that it is the case, but I am struggling to match it to the description here:  http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2041-210x.2012.00257.x/abstract

I will really appreciate your comments.

Best regards

Pablo

messages.subject: simNmix visualization
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am running a simulation for N-mixture models according to section 6.6 in the AHM book (page 245). I'm looking at the differences between 30 and 50 sites, with each visited twice. Mean lambda was 2, 3, or 4, as we're focused on uncommon bird species. When I graph the results with a smoothing spline, the default is unlimited degrees of freedom. The result is that some graphs include a lot of fluctuation which seems to make them harder to interpret. I also graphed them with a set number of degrees of freedom so that there would be the same number across all plots. Is it ok to set the number of degrees of freedom like this or is it misleading in some way? It seems to make the graphs more comparable and the trends depicted make sense. I'm new to smoothers though so am not quite sure.

R code and a word document with graphs (default and 8 degrees of freedom) are attached.

Thanks!
-Wendy

Hi Wendy,

The analytical solution should be some sort of decay towards the true value of lambda rather than a polynomial-looking curve, I would think.  Fixing the df on the smoother is probably fine for visualizing the relationship, or not fixing the df but also not taking the humps too seriously.
